statement: The literature on digital infrastructure for research-process management is an assembly of partially connected strands (scientific workflows, research data management, provenance, research information systems, open science, version control), not one field.
The field is output-biased: data management (50.8% of the corpus) and analysis/workflow (41.9%) dominate; idea/question is 3.7% and provenance 7.0%.
Seven of fifteen research-lifecycle stages are thinly covered by the literature: idea, question, planning, ethics review, post-publication traceability, cross-stage coordination, governance.
Annual output rises nearly tenfold 2008 to 2024 (60 to 585); 2025 is only partially indexed and is reported with a caveat and a 2008-2024 trimmed series.
Two independent methods converge: an AI deep-search synthesis of 52 review/synthesis papers (Track B) and a 5,139-work OpenAlex+arXiv bibliometric corpus (Track A) both show the same output bias.

Fifteen research management requirements (RM1-RM15) were derived from the literature, concentrated in four categories: Traceability 4, Documentation 3, Collaboration 2, one each for Planning, Execution, Artifact management, Automation, Output management.
Three requirements are High-importance but weak in literature attention - the differentiators: RM1 research planning, RM2 research-question management, RM5 decision traceability.
The requirements are interdependent: RM10 provenance consumes RM2, RM4, RM5, RM8, RM9; RM11 transparency is an emergent property of RM4, RM5, RM8, RM10.
GitHub supports 13 of 15 requirements at Partial or better and 7 at Direct, with none unsupported; mean support 2.43/3 for the core 14 (2.33 for the full 15).

Support is Direct where research work resembles software engineering: task management, review-based collaboration, communication, version control, documentation, transparency, automation (category means 3.0).
Support is Partial or Limited for research-specific traceability (RM2 Limited, RM5 and RM10 Partial), planning (RM1 Partial) and governance (RM15 Limited).
The differentiator requirements have mean GitHub support 1.67 versus 2.50 for the rest - the upstream gap is real on the tool side and mirrors the RQ1 literature gap.
Five requirements (RM8, RM9, RM12, RM14, RM15) cannot be met by GitHub alone and require complementary external infrastructure.
The lifecycle-coverage profile is comparatively flat (2.1-2.4) but lowest at idea (2.12) and question (2.25) and highest at literature, analysis and manuscript - the same shape as the RQ1 gap.
Issues and the Git repository carry most of the framework; Projects, Actions, Discussions, Branches and Releases each contribute to only a few requirements.
The headline finding is robust to rubric choice: capping convention-heavy support at Limited lowers the mean 2.33 to 2.13 but leaves the qualitative conclusion unchanged.
The covered capabilities organise into a 15-component, 5-layer reference architecture in which GitHub is a coordination and traceability layer, not a container for every activity.

One component (B3 Linkage Discipline) and four named conventions are the framework's distinctive contribution over a plain GitHub repository; they are what lift RM1, RM2, RM5 and RM10 from raw features to research-usable support.
The architecture is operationalised as a 33-file, discipline-independent GitHub template in which every requirement RM1-RM15 is served by at least one file or configuration step.

In the self-referential implementation, 13 of 15 components were exercised natively or partially (8 during the single-author phase; the activity tracker, review workflow, release process, governance and transparency components after one live cycle and making the repository public); the documentation, decision-log and version-control spine works with near-zero coordination overhead.

After one live Issue->PR->Release cycle and making the repository public, the six-dimension evaluation scores 1.86/2 overall (1.85/2 for the twenty observed sub-scores); coverage, documentation, organization and transparency at 2.0, usability lowest at 1.50 (configuration cost and technical-literacy barrier).
Against a fragmented workflow, the framework's benefit is concentrated in linking artifacts that would otherwise stay disconnected; its cost is concentrated in the coordination layer.
The framework maps the upstream research-process gap but does not close it: RM1, RM2 and RM5 remain Partial or Limited even with the prescribed conventions.

The coordination layer's collaborative benefit is unproven: it was run once end-to-end by a single author, so multi-author review and communication (RM6, RM7) are untested, and the configuration and technical-literacy costs (E6) remain.

The evaluation is single-case and self-referential, scored by a single coder; an independent LLM re-code of all 53 coded decisions (RE->RM, support levels, sub-scores) agreed at 96.2% (Cohen's kappa 0.83-1.00 per unit) with two adjacent-category disagreements that change no reported conclusion, but no human second coder was available.

The primary bibliometric corpus is OpenAlex plus arXiv; a Scopus and Web of Science cross-check (18,250 raw, 13,586 de-duplicated in-window records) shares 22% of its DOIs with the corpus, the divergence being a characterised precision tail of tool-citing papers rather than missed core literature, with a broad-query precision estimate of about 0.94.
About a third of the coverage rests on mandatory convention rather than native features, as the stricter-rubric mean of 2.13 shows.

GitHub is not a complete research infrastructure: persistent identifiers and preservation (Zenodo), computational environments (containers), large datasets (data repositories) and institutional governance are all external.
Practical guidance: adopt the record and version-control spine first (low cost, high value); add the coordination layer when the project has collaborators.

For the field: the upstream traceability gap - convergent across RQ1 and RQ3 - is a concrete target for tool development and for reporting standards on decision records and research-question provenance.
For open science: GitHub-based process management is the upstream half of a GitHub-Zenodo-ORCID research lifecycle, complementing output archiving rather than replacing it.

Answer to the main research question: GitHub can serve as an integrated coordination and traceability layer for a substantial part of the research lifecycle - strong from execution to output, weak upstream, dependent on complementary infrastructure - mapping the research-process-management gap rather than closing it.
